title: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles

endcard.line: Pictures: Constituent Assembly of India (public domain); Beohar Rammanohar Sinha; David Castor (public domain); MohitSingh (CC BY 3.0)

segments.say: India's Constitution makes two kinds of promises. Some you can take to court. Others, you can't. Why?

left.title: Fundamental Rights
items: Limit what the State may do

right.title: Directive Principles
items: Goals the State should work for

segments.say: Fundamental Rights, in Part Three, are enforceable: a court can strike down a law that breaks them. Directive Principles, in Part Four, are goals for the State, and no court can force them.

anim.title: Examples
items: Principle: equal pay for equal work (Art. 39)

segments.say: Equality before law and free speech are rights. Equal pay for equal work and village panchayats began as directive principles.
Why the difference? In nineteen fifty, a poor new country couldn't promise every goal at once. So the framers called the principles fundamental in governing, but left them to the State's pace.

items.text: Golaknath: rights can't be cut down
Minerva Mills: harmony between the two is itself basic structure

segments.say: Which wins when they clash? After years of cases, the Supreme Court said in Minerva Mills, nineteen eighty, that the balance between the two is itself part of the basic structure.
Today courts read them together. The right to life has been read with directive principles to include education, health and a clean environment.

anim.title: For your answer
items: Minerva Mills: balance is basic structure

segments.say: For GS Two: rights are justiciable, principles are not, says Article thirty-seven. And Minerva Mills says the two must stay in balance.

sources: Constitution of India, Part III (Articles 12–35) and Part IV (Articles 36–51); Article 37: directive principles not enforceable by any court but fundamental in the governance of the country; Articles 14, 19, 39(d), 40
Minerva Mills Ltd v Union of India (1980) 3 SCC 625: harmony and balance between Parts III and IV is a basic feature
I.C. Golaknath v State of Punjab (1967); Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala (1973)
NCERT Class 11, 'Indian Constitution at Work', ch. 2 (Rights in the Indian Constitution)
